question: Why do you want to study supply chain and logistics?
lookingFor: A specific, personal reason for the field, not a vague claim about liking business or organisation.

bullets: Point to a concrete moment or experience that sparked the interest
Show you understand what the field actually involves day to day
Connect it to something you want to build a career doing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During the pandemic I watched my uncle's small pharmacy run out of basic medicines for weeks while shelves elsewhere sat full, and that gap between where things are made and where they're needed stuck with me. I started reading about how companies route goods and manage inventory, and I realised it's really a puzzle of trade-offs between cost, speed, and risk. I want to study it properly because I want to be the person who designs systems that don't break when the world does.

commonMistakes: Saying it purely because the job market looks strong
Confusing supply chain with just delivery drivers or trucks
Giving an answer with no personal story behind it
followUps: What part of that experience made you curious rather than just frustrated?

question: Why our supply chain and logistics program specifically, rather than a general business degree?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course structure and what makes it distinct from a generic business degree.

bullets: Name a specific module, simulation lab, or industry link the course offers
Explain why the specialised focus suits how you want to learn
Show you compared it against alternatives rather than applying broadly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at three business programs and yours is the only one with a dedicated logistics simulation lab in second year, where students actually run a warehouse network under disruption scenarios. I don't want supply chain to be one module buried inside a general business degree, I want it to be the spine of what I study, with electives in procurement and transportation economics built around it. Your partnership with a regional freight company for the capstone project is exactly the kind of applied exposure I'm looking for.

commonMistakes: Praising the university's reputation with no course-specific detail
Treating supply chain as interchangeable with any business major
Not being able to name a single module or feature
followUps: What would you want to get out of that capstone project specifically?

question: Do you have any experience, work or otherwise, that connects to supply chain or logistics?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific experience with reflection on what it taught the applicant, even if informal or small-scale.

bullets: Describe a concrete experience, even a small or informal one
Explain what you actually did or observed, not just that you were present
Reflect on what it taught you about the field
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I did a two-week shadowing placement at a regional distribution centre for a grocery chain, where I sat in on their inventory planning meetings and watched them react to a delayed shipment in real time. What struck me was how much of the job is forecasting and contingency planning rather than just moving boxes, they had three backup suppliers lined up before the delay even became a problem. It made me want to understand the mathematics behind those forecasts, which is part of why I'm applying now.

commonMistakes: Claiming experience that is too vague to describe in detail
Only describing what the company did, with no personal takeaway
Overstating a brief exposure as deep expertise
followUps: What surprised you most about how that operation actually worked?

question: Have you read anything, a book, article, or case study, that shaped how you think about supply chains?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine independent reading with the ability to summarise and react to it, not just name-dropping a title.

bullets: Name a specific source, not a vague genre
Summarise the core idea in your own words
Say how it changed or sharpened your thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Yossi Sheffi's book on resilient supply chains after the Suez Canal blockage made headlines, and what stayed with me was his point that redundancy, having backup suppliers or routes, looks wasteful right up until the moment it saves you. Before that I'd assumed efficient meant lean and single-sourced, but he argues that resilience is actually a competitive advantage, not just an insurance cost. It made me want to understand how companies actually quantify that trade-off instead of just talking about it in principle.

commonMistakes: Naming a title without being able to discuss any content
Only mentioning news headlines with no deeper source
Reciting a summary with no personal reaction
followUps: Do you agree with that argument, or do you see a flaw in it?

question: How would you explain the difference between logistics and supply chain management?
lookingFor: A clear conceptual distinction showing logistics is a subset of the broader supply chain function.

bullets: Define logistics as the movement and storage of goods
Define supply chain management as the broader coordination of all parties
Give an example that shows how the two relate
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Logistics is really about the physical movement and storage of goods, things like transportation, warehousing, and order fulfilment. Supply chain management is the bigger picture, it's coordinating everyone involved from raw material suppliers through manufacturing, distribution, and the end customer, including decisions about sourcing and demand planning that logistics doesn't cover on its own. So if a company decides which supplier to use and how much to order, that's supply chain management, but once the goods are actually moving, that's logistics executing the plan.

commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as fully interchangeable
Defining logistics too broadly so it swallows supply chain management
Giving a definition with no example to anchor it
followUps: Where would procurement fit into that picture?

question: What is the bullwhip effect, and why does it happen?
lookingFor: Understanding that small demand fluctuations amplify as they move upstream, plus an idea of why.

bullets: Explain that small changes in customer demand get amplified further up the chain
Give at least one cause, such as order batching, delays, or overreaction to shortages
Mention a real or plausible consequence, like overstocking or stockouts
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The bullwhip effect is when a small change in actual customer demand gets progressively exaggerated as you move up the chain from retailer to distributor to manufacturer. It happens partly because each link reacts to the order it receives from the one below rather than the true end demand, and partly because of batching orders, promotions, and the natural lag between ordering and receiving stock. The result is that manufacturers can end up wildly overproducing or underproducing relative to what customers actually wanted, which is why sharing real demand data across the chain matters so much.

commonMistakes: Describing it as simple demand volatility with no amplification mechanism
Confusing cause and effect
Giving no real-world consequence
followUps: What's one way companies try to reduce the bullwhip effect?

question: What is just-in-time inventory, and what is its main risk?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of the JIT concept and awareness that it trades cost efficiency for resilience.

bullets: Define JIT as receiving goods only as they're needed to minimise holding inventory
State the main benefit, lower storage cost and less waste
State the main risk, vulnerability to any disruption in the supply line
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Just-in-time inventory means ordering and receiving materials only right before they're needed in production, instead of holding large stockpiles in a warehouse. Toyota built its whole production system around it, and it cuts storage costs and reduces waste from unsold or obsolete stock. The catch is that it leaves almost no buffer, so if one supplier is delayed or a port shuts down, the whole line can stop within days, which is exactly what happened to a lot of automakers during the pandemic chip shortage.

commonMistakes: Describing JIT without mentioning the resilience trade-off
Confusing JIT with EOQ or safety stock
Giving no real example of when it failed
followUps: How would you balance JIT efficiency against the need for resilience?

question: What's the difference between a push and a pull supply chain strategy?
lookingFor: Correct distinction between forecast-driven and demand-driven production, with an example of each.

bullets: Define push as producing based on forecasts ahead of actual demand
Define pull as producing or replenishing in response to actual demand
Give an example or hybrid case, such as Dell's build-to-order model
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A push strategy means a company produces and ships goods based on a demand forecast before any order actually comes in, which is how most fast fashion and grocery stock works. A pull strategy means production only starts once an actual customer order triggers it, which is closer to how Dell built computers to order rather than stockpiling finished laptops. Most real supply chains are actually a hybrid, they might push standard components into a regional warehouse and then pull the final assembly once the specific order arrives, which balances speed against the risk of overproducing.

commonMistakes: Only giving definitions with no real company example
Missing that many chains are hybrid rather than purely one or the other
Confusing pull systems with reverse logistics
followUps: Which industries do you think benefit most from a pull strategy, and why?

question: Can you talk through a recent supply chain disruption you followed, and what caused it?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real, specific disruption with an understanding of its underlying cause, not just headline recall.

bullets: Name a specific, real disruption with roughly correct facts
Explain the underlying mechanism, not just the news headline
Note a downstream consequence or lesson companies drew from it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I followed the Suez Canal blockage in 2021 closely, when the Ever Given ran aground and shut the canal for about six days. What made it interesting to me wasn't just the single ship, it was that the canal carries around twelve percent of global trade, so even a short blockage backed up hundreds of vessels and rippled through shipping schedules for months afterward. It pushed a lot of companies to seriously reconsider single-route dependency and think harder about diversifying shipping lanes and even nearshoring some production, which is the kind of resilience thinking I find genuinely interesting.

commonMistakes: Getting basic facts about the event wrong
Only describing what happened with no analysis of cause or consequence
Picking an event you clearly know very little about
followUps: What would you have advised a company to do differently in response?

question: How can supply chains be made more environmentally sustainable, and what trade-offs does that involve?
lookingFor: A balanced answer that names concrete levers and honestly acknowledges the cost or complexity trade-offs.

bullets: Name at least two concrete levers, such as route optimisation, packaging, or supplier vetting
Acknowledge that sustainability choices often carry a cost or speed trade-off
Show awareness that sustainability claims need real measurement, not just marketing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There are a few real levers, consolidating shipments to cut empty truck miles, switching to rail or sea over air freight where the timeline allows, and vetting suppliers on labour and environmental standards rather than just price. The honest trade-off is that most of these cost more or take longer in the short term, so a company has to decide how much margin or speed it's willing to give up. What interests me is that some companies are finding sustainability actually pays off through efficiency, less waste and fewer near-empty shipments usually means lower cost too, but that's not automatic and needs real measurement rather than just claiming it.

commonMistakes: Treating sustainability as free with no acknowledged trade-off
Giving only vague buzzwords with no concrete lever
Ignoring the measurement or greenwashing problem
followUps: How would you convince a cost-focused executive to invest in this?

question: What role do you think technology, like data analytics or tracking systems, plays in modern supply chains?
lookingFor: Concrete grasp of specific technologies and their function, not generic enthusiasm about digitalisation.

bullets: Name a specific technology, such as ERP systems, IoT sensors, or demand forecasting software
Explain the concrete problem it solves
Show a realistic view of its limits, not blind techno-optimism
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Real-time tracking through IoT sensors on containers has changed a lot, companies can now see exactly where a shipment is and reroute before a delay becomes a crisis, rather than finding out after the fact. Demand forecasting software that pulls in weather, social trends, and historical sales lets retailers plan inventory far more precisely than a spreadsheet ever could. But I don't think technology solves everything on its own, it's still only as good as the data feeding it, and a system that isn't shared across partners in the chain can just create a more precise version of the same blind spots.

commonMistakes: Speaking only in buzzwords like AI or blockchain with no specifics
Assuming technology automatically fixes coordination problems
Naming a technology without explaining what problem it solves
followUps: Can you think of a situation where more data wouldn't actually help?

question: What is third-party logistics, and why would a company use one instead of managing its own warehousing and shipping?
lookingFor: Correct definition of 3PL with a reasonable understanding of the cost and expertise trade-off behind outsourcing.

bullets: Define 3PL as outsourcing logistics functions to a specialist provider
Give the main reason companies use them, cost, scale, or expertise
Note a trade-off, such as losing direct control
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A third-party logistics provider is a company a business hires to handle warehousing, transportation, or fulfilment on its behalf, rather than building and running that infrastructure itself. A smaller retailer might not have the volume to justify its own fleet or warehouse network, so using a 3PL lets it access established infrastructure and expertise at a lower fixed cost, and scale up or down more easily. The trade-off is that you give up some direct control over how your product is handled, so companies usually keep tight service-level agreements to make sure quality doesn't slip.

commonMistakes: Confusing 3PL with a single delivery courier
Only giving the definition without the underlying business reason
Missing the control trade-off entirely
followUps: What would make a company decide to bring logistics back in-house instead?

question: Why can't a company simply keep as much inventory as possible to avoid ever running out of stock?
lookingFor: Understanding of holding cost, obsolescence, and capital tied up as counterweights to stockout risk.

bullets: Name holding costs, warehousing, insurance, spoilage or obsolescence
Mention capital tied up that could be used elsewhere
Frame it as a genuine balancing act, not a simple maximum or minimum
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Holding inventory isn't free, you're paying for warehouse space, insurance, and in some cases the risk that the product spoils or becomes obsolete before it sells, think of unsold smartphones after a new model launches. There's also an opportunity cost, every dollar tied up in stock sitting on a shelf is a dollar that isn't being used to grow the business elsewhere. So the real question isn't maximising stock, it's finding the point where the cost of holding extra inventory roughly balances the cost of running out, which is really what concepts like safety stock and reorder points are trying to calculate.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning stockout risk with no counterweight
Treating storage as costless
Giving no sense that this is a calculated balance rather than a guess
followUps: How would a seasonal product change that calculation?

question: If you had to ship goods internationally, what factors would decide whether you use air, sea, rail, or road freight?
lookingFor: A clear sense of the speed versus cost trade-off across modes, with sensible reasoning for when each fits.

bullets: Identify speed and cost as the core trade-off
Mention at least one other factor, like volume, distance, or product perishability
Give a sensible example of which mode fits which situation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The biggest trade-off is speed against cost, air freight is by far the fastest but also the most expensive per unit of weight, while sea freight is much cheaper but can take weeks. So a company shipping something high-value and time-sensitive, like consumer electronics ahead of a launch, might eat the air freight cost, while bulk raw materials like grain or steel almost always go by sea because the volume makes the cost per unit tiny. Distance and infrastructure matter too, rail is efficient for large inland volumes where the track network exists, and road usually handles the final leg because it's the only mode flexible enough to reach an actual doorstep.

commonMistakes: Only naming the modes without explaining the trade-off between them
Ignoring product characteristics like perishability or value density
Assuming one mode is simply better in all cases
followUps: How would a perishable product like fresh produce change your answer?

question: What is reverse logistics, and why has it become more important recently?
lookingFor: Correct definition tied to returns and recycling, with a link to a real driver like e-commerce growth.

bullets: Define reverse logistics as the process of moving goods from customer back to seller or manufacturer
Give examples like returns, repairs, or recycling
Link its growing importance to a real driver, such as e-commerce return rates
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Reverse logistics is the flow of goods moving backward through the supply chain, from the customer back to the retailer or manufacturer, whether that's for a return, a repair, or end-of-life recycling. It's become a much bigger deal because online shopping has driven return rates way up compared to in-store purchases, since customers order multiple sizes or styles knowing they can send back what doesn't fit. Managing that well matters a lot financially too, a badly designed returns process can eat a huge chunk of margin, so companies are investing seriously in things like resale channels and better return sorting to recover value instead of just writing the product off.

commonMistakes: Defining it only as returns with no mention of repair or recycling
Missing the e-commerce driver behind its growing importance
Treating reverse logistics as a minor operational detail
followUps: How would you design a returns process to minimise cost while keeping customers happy?

question: How would a company go about identifying and managing risk in its supply chain?
lookingFor: A structured way of thinking about risk identification and mitigation, not just naming that risk exists.

bullets: Mention mapping the supply chain to find single points of failure
Name at least one mitigation strategy, like dual sourcing or safety stock
Acknowledge that not all risk can be eliminated, only managed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by mapping the whole chain to find single points of failure, a supplier you rely on for a critical component with no backup is a much bigger risk than a commodity input you can source from ten places. From there, common mitigations include dual or multi-sourcing key inputs, holding strategic safety stock for the most critical items, and building contractual flexibility with suppliers so you're not locked into rigid volumes. I don't think a company can eliminate risk entirely, it's more about deciding which risks are worth the cost of insuring against and which ones you're willing to accept and just monitor closely.

commonMistakes: Saying 'have a backup plan' with no structured approach
Ignoring the cost trade-off of risk mitigation
Treating risk as something to eliminate rather than manage
followUps: How would you decide which risks are worth mitigating and which to just accept?

question: What kind of role in supply chain or logistics do you see yourself in after you graduate?
lookingFor: A grounded, informed sense of direction that shows the applicant understands the range of roles in the field.

bullets: Name a plausible entry point or direction, not an implausibly senior title
Show awareness of what that role actually involves day to day
Connect it back to specific coursework or skills the degree would build
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd like to start in demand planning or procurement, somewhere close to the analytical side where I'm forecasting and negotiating rather than purely operational, and build toward a role in supply chain strategy over time. I know that means starting with a lot of spreadsheet and forecasting work before I get near strategic decisions, and honestly that's fine with me, I want to understand the data before I try to shape the bigger picture. That's part of why the analytics and procurement modules in this course matter to me specifically, they're the exact skills I think that early-career work would demand.

commonMistakes: Naming an unrealistically senior title like Chief Supply Chain Officer straight out of university
Giving an answer with no connection to what the course actually teaches
Being so vague it could describe any business career
followUps: What skill do you think you'd need to develop most to succeed in that role?

question: If you discovered a low-cost supplier your company relied on was using labour practices you found ethically troubling, what would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning weighing cost, responsibility, and stakeholders, not a snap answer either way.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine tension between cost, jobs, and ethics
Propose a reasoned path, such as verifying findings and pushing for remediation before cutting ties outright
Show awareness of second-order effects, like workers losing income entirely if the contract is simply pulled
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct would be to verify the findings properly rather than act on a rumour, because a wrong accusation has real consequences for real people too. If it's confirmed, I don't think the right answer is necessarily to cut the supplier immediately, since that can leave workers with no income at all, I'd want the company to use its leverage to demand a remediation plan with a clear timeline first. But if the supplier refused to change or the practices were severe, like forced labour, then I think the company has to be willing to walk away, because using cost savings from serious labour abuse isn't something a business should quietly accept just because switching suppliers is expensive.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to cutting the supplier with no consideration of worker impact
Excusing the practice purely on cost grounds
Giving no structured reasoning, just a gut verdict
followUps: How would your answer change if switching suppliers meant a 30 percent cost increase?

question: What are the trade-offs between sourcing materials globally versus sourcing them locally?
lookingFor: A balanced view weighing cost against lead time, resilience, and control, not a one-sided preference.

bullets: Name cost as the usual driver toward global sourcing
Name lead time and resilience as the case for local sourcing
Show awareness this is a live strategic debate, referencing nearshoring or reshoring trends
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Global sourcing usually wins on raw cost, labour and materials can be significantly cheaper in certain regions, which is why so much manufacturing shifted overseas over the last few decades. But it comes with longer lead times, higher transportation emissions, and much less resilience, if a factory across the world shuts down you find out days later and have far fewer options to react quickly. That's part of why there's been a real push toward nearshoring recently, companies are willing to pay a bit more to source closer to home in exchange for shorter lead times and the ability to actually see and influence what's happening in their supply chain.

commonMistakes: Treating global sourcing as simply better because it's cheaper
Ignoring current nearshoring or reshoring trends
Giving no concrete example of either approach
followUps: What kind of product would you say is a poor candidate for global sourcing?

question: Have you come across concepts like Lean or Six Sigma? What do you understand them to mean in a supply chain context?
lookingFor: Basic but accurate grasp of waste reduction and variation reduction as applied to supply chain operations.

bullets: Define Lean as focused on eliminating waste in a process
Define Six Sigma as focused on reducing variation and defects
Give a supply chain example where one might apply
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: From what I've read, Lean is about identifying and removing waste in a process, things like unnecessary movement, waiting time, or excess inventory that doesn't add value for the customer, which is really where the just-in-time philosophy came from. Six Sigma is more about reducing variation and defects using statistical methods, aiming for a process that's consistently accurate rather than just fast. In a warehouse, you might use Lean thinking to redesign the picking route to cut unnecessary walking, and Six Sigma to figure out why a certain percentage of shipments keep arriving with the wrong item, which are two different but complementary kinds of improvement.

commonMistakes: Treating Lean and Six Sigma as the same thing
Only naming the terms with no working definition
Giving no concrete application to logistics or supply chain
followUps: Which of the two do you think would be more useful in a fast-changing e-commerce warehouse?

question: If a retailer asked you where to build a new regional warehouse, what factors would you weigh in that decision?
lookingFor: Structured case-style reasoning across multiple factors, showing this is a genuine optimisation problem.

bullets: Mention proximity to customer demand and transportation infrastructure
Mention labour cost and availability, and land or facility cost
Acknowledge it's a multi-factor optimisation, not a single deciding variable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start with where the customer demand is actually concentrated, since being closer to that demand cuts delivery time and transportation cost, which usually matters more than almost anything else for a retailer. Then I'd look at infrastructure, is it near a major highway or rail line, and at labour, is there a workforce available at a reasonable cost in that area. Land and facility costs matter too, but I wouldn't treat any single factor as decisive, it's really about running the numbers on total landed cost across a few candidate sites and seeing which one balances speed to customer against operating cost the best, which is exactly the kind of network design problem I'd want to learn to model properly.

commonMistakes: Naming only one factor, like cost or location, as if it decides everything
Ignoring customer demand concentration entirely
Giving a vague answer with no sense of how to actually weigh the factors against each other
followUps: How would your answer change if the retailer needed same-day delivery in that region?

question: If a store sells 100 units of a product a week and it takes two weeks for a new order to arrive, roughly how much stock should be on hand when they place a reorder, and why might they want more than that?
lookingFor: Ability to reason through a basic reorder point calculation and articulate why safety stock is added on top.

bullets: Calculate the baseline reorder point as demand rate times lead time, 100 times 2 equals 200 units
Explain that 200 covers only expected demand with no room for variability
Explain why safety stock is added on top, to cover demand spikes or supplier delays
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If they sell 100 units a week and the lead time is two weeks, then by the time a new order arrives they'll have sold through roughly 200 units, so the baseline reorder point is around 200 units of stock on hand. But that number assumes demand stays perfectly steady and the supplier is never late, which isn't realistic, so in practice you'd want to add safety stock on top, maybe another 50 to 100 units depending on how variable demand actually is and how reliable that supplier has historically been. The exact safety stock number would really come from looking at historical demand variability and the supplier's delivery consistency rather than just guessing.

commonMistakes: Getting the basic multiplication wrong or skipping the calculation entirely
Stopping at the baseline number with no mention of safety stock
Giving a safety stock figure with no reasoning behind it
followUps: What would you want to know to calculate the safety stock more precisely?

question: What's a famous supply chain failure you find interesting, and what do you think the company should have done differently?
lookingFor: Genuine familiarity with a real case plus independent judgement on what could have been done better.

bullets: Name a real, specific case with roughly correct details
Explain what actually went wrong
Offer your own view on what should have been done differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I find the Boeing 787 Dreamliner's early production delays fascinating, they outsourced huge portions of the aircraft's design and manufacturing to suppliers around the world to cut cost and speed things up, but ended up with years of delays because they'd underestimated how much coordination that level of outsourcing would actually require. If I'd been advising them, I'd have pushed for a much more staged rollout of outsourcing, proving the coordination model worked on a smaller, less critical component first before betting the whole aircraft's structure on it. It taught me that outsourcing isn't just a cost decision, the complexity of managing that many external relationships is its own real cost that's easy to underestimate.

commonMistakes: Getting basic facts about the case wrong
Only describing the failure with no independent view on what should change
Picking a case too obscure or unclear to actually discuss
followUps: Do you think that same risk applies to how companies use AI tools in their supply chains today?

question: This course involves a lot of group case studies and simulations. What would you personally bring to a team working through a supply chain problem?
lookingFor: A specific, honest self-assessment of strengths tied to the collaborative and analytical nature of the course.

bullets: Name a specific strength, not a generic claim like 'hard worker'
Back it with a concrete example of using that strength in a group setting
Connect it to what group case work in this field actually needs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm the person in a group who tends to push us to actually check our numbers before we present, in a school economics project I caught an error in our group's cost model two days before submission that would have thrown off our whole recommendation. I think that habit of stress-testing assumptions matters a lot in supply chain case work specifically, because these problems usually look clean on the surface until you dig into the actual data, like lead times or demand variability, that most people gloss over. I also enjoy the coordinating role, making sure everyone's piece of an analysis actually fits together into one coherent recommendation.

commonMistakes: Giving a generic answer like 'I'm a team player' with no example
Claiming a strength with no evidence it's genuinely true
Describing a strength unrelated to analytical or collaborative case work
followUps: Tell me about a time that strength actually caused friction with a teammate.

subtopic: Supply chain vs other business fields
question: Supply chain roles can seem less visible than areas like marketing or finance. Why does this field appeal to you more than those?
lookingFor: A genuine comparative reason for the field grounded in what the applicant actually wants to do, not a dismissal of other fields.

bullets: Show respect for adjacent fields rather than dismissing them
Articulate specifically what draws you to supply chain over them
Ground it in a concrete preference, like problem type or the tangibility of the work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think marketing or finance are less interesting, a few of my friends applying this year are drawn to exactly those fields and I get why. What pulls me toward supply chain specifically is that the problems are tangible, you can trace a decision about where to source a component all the way through to a physical product arriving on a shelf, and I like that the results aren't abstract. I also like that it sits at the intersection of a lot of disciplines, some data analysis, some negotiation, some operations, rather than living entirely inside one lens, which suits how I like to think.

commonMistakes: Putting down other fields to make this one look better by comparison
Giving an answer that could apply equally to any business field
Failing to identify what specifically differs about supply chain work
followUps: What's a problem type from another field you'd still want to bring into supply chain work?
